 Two 64-Year-Olds Each Earn $40,000 From the Same Wells as Oil Falls 13% in a Week: the Royalty Owner Keeps Every Social Security Check, While the Working-Interest Partner Gives Up $7,220
 Gerelyn Terzo Thu, November 19, 2026 at 5:35 PM MST 6 min read CL=F +0.27% 
 Quick Read 
 Social Security's earnings test counts working-interest profits as self-employment income but ignores royalties, so a working-interest partner earning $40,000 loses about $7,000 in 2027 benefits while a royalty owner loses nothing. 
 Withheld benefits return slowly through a recalculated, higher monthly check at full retirement age, and updating the earnings estimate as oil prices fall prevents excess withholding. 
 Royalty income still raises taxes on benefits, while working-interest profits face 15.3% self-employment tax; waiting until full retirement age may suit partners, since early-claiming reductions are permanent.

 Two 64-year-old neighbors in oil country each collected $40,000 this year from the same cluster of wells. One inherited the mineral rights and receives royalty checks. The other bought a working interest, which means owning a piece of the operation itself and paying a share of the drilling and lease costs. Both started Social Security early, and both are watching oil prices fall. 
 24/7 Wall St. The slide has been steep. West Texas crude, the U.S. benchmark, dropped from $110 a barrel on October 19 to $90 on November 11, and at last check is hovering near the $80 threshold. Economists are bracing for a global supply surplus. Both neighbors will see smaller checks. Next year, though, only one of them will also see smaller Social Security deposits, and the reason comes down to a single label on their income. 
 Why the Royalty Owner Keeps Every Check 
 Anyone who claims Social Security before full retirement age (FRA), which is 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later, runs into the earnings test. It counts paychecks and self-employment profits. It ignores investment income.

 Social Security treats net earnings from a working interest as self-employment income. In the agency's eyes, the partner runs a small oil business. The royalty owner simply collects rent on minerals in the ground, and oil royalties are investment income that doesn't count. 
 Here is how that plays out in 2027, when both neighbors are below the age for full benefits all year. The exempt amount rises to $25,560, and the agency withholds $1 in benefits for every $2 in earnings above the limit. 
 With $40,000 of net working-interest profit, the partner gives up $7,220. With $40,000 of royalties, the neighbor gives up nothing. 
 To put that in checks: the average retired worker will receive $2,170 a month after the 3.6% cost-of-living raise for 2027. 
 At that size, $7,220 equals more than three months of benefits. The agency generally holds back whole checks early in the year until it has collected what it is owed, so the partner could open the mailbox in January, February and March and find nothing. 
 Withheld Money Comes Back, Slowly 
 Once the partner reaches 67, Social Security recalculates the benefit to give credit for the months withheld. The monthly check rises for good, and the $7,220 trickles back over many years. If cash flow is tight at 65, that slow return offers little comfort. 
 Falling oil prices help a little here. Every $2 of lost profit cuts the withholding by $1. If lower prices shrink the partner's 2027 net earnings, updating the earnings estimate on file with Social Security keeps the agency from holding back more than necessary. A stale estimate from a $110 oil year could cost several extra checks that come back only after the annual reconciliation. 
 How Taxes Still Reach the Royalty Owner 
 The royalty owner gets out of the earnings test but still owes income tax. Royalties are generally reported on Schedule E, and that income counts toward the formula that determines how much of each benefit payment is taxable. At $40,000 of royalties on top of benefits, a large piece of those checks will likely be taxed. 
 The partner bears a heavier load. Working-interest profits face the 15.3% self-employment tax rate on top of income tax. That tax brings one quiet benefit: those earnings go on the partner's Social Security record. If they rank among the partner's highest-earning years, the benefit gets recalculated upward. 
 Decide These Two Questions Before You Claim 
 Find out which label your income bears. Before claiming early, check whether your oil income comes from royalties or a working interest. If you're a working-interest partner, run the withholding math with the current year's limit, and redo it whenever prices move sharply. 
 Remember which cost is permanent. Unlike withheld benefits, the reduction for claiming early never goes away. For a partner whose checks will be partly withheld anyway, waiting until the age for full benefits to claim may cost very little and lock in a larger check for life. 
 Ownership structures vary, and some arrangements blur the line between royalty and working interest, so it's worth having a tax professional confirm how your specific interest is classified when you prepare your return.
